The Eurasian sparrowhawk (Accipiter nisus) exhibits pronounced sexual size dimorphism, a trait characteristic of many accipitrid raptors. Adult females attain a substantially larger body size, with the maximum recorded adult body mass reaching 310 grams [Wwi = 310 grams], though individuals can range from 185 to 342 grams depending on local prey abundance and geographic latitude. In contrast, males are notably more diminutive, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 180 grams [Wwi = 180 grams], with a documented range of 110 to 196 grams across their Palearctic distribution. This size disparity is linked to niche partitioning, where the larger females can take avian prey up to the size of woodpigeons, while the smaller males predominantly hunt smaller passerines. The energetic demands of flight impose a strong upper constraint on male mass, a pattern that is especially pronounced in woodland habitats where maneuverability is at a premium.

Reproductive investment in this species follows a pattern typical of long-lived raptors. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of the active breeding season, at an ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], females produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. Each reproductive event yields 4 to 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4 to 5 eggs per clutch], a moderate clutch size that reflects the trade-off between offspring number and the intensive parental care required for altricial development. The eggs are incubated primarily by the female, who is provisioned by her mate during the nesting period. This combination of annual clutch frequency and per-clutch output allows the reconstruction of potential annual fecundity. In productive years with high prey availability, some females may attempt a replacement clutch if the first is lost to predation.

The timing of developmental milestones in the Eurasian sparrowhawk is tightly coupled to the incubation temperature, which is maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] by the attentive brooding of the female. At this stable thermal regime, hatching occurs after an incubation period of 33 days [ab = 33 days], a duration that aligns with that of other medium-sized accipiters at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. The newly hatched nestling emerges at a wet weight of just 16.5 grams [Wwb = 16.5 grams], representing a minute fraction of the adult female's mass and underscoring the extreme altriciality of the species. This initial body mass is almost entirely yolk-derived, and the chick is entirely dependent on parental brooding for thermoregulation during its first week of life. The rapid growth phase that follows is fueled by a diet of plucked passerine prey delivered at frequent intervals by the male, while the female remains at the nest to tear food into manageable portions.

A predictable sequence of post-natal developmental events unfolds under the elevated body temperatures of the nestling, typically sustained at 40 °C [T = 40 °C] during periods of active parental attendance. However, despite reaching physiological puberty at this relatively early age, most individuals do not breed immediately; the time since birth at first brood, or age at first successful reproduction, is typically deferred until 365 days after birth [tR = 365 days after birth], coinciding with the following breeding season when territory acquisition is possible at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C].

Longevity records for the Eurasian sparrowhawk indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 20.2 years [am = approximately 20.2 years], a value established from ring-recovery data and reported for individuals maintained under favorable conditions at a typical active metabolic temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This substantial lifespan is characteristic of a slow life-history pace, where high adult survival compensates for the relatively modest annual reproductive output of a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year] with 4 to 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4 to 5 eggs per clutch]. Mortality is highest during the first year of life, particularly in the post-fledging dispersal phase when naive juveniles face starvation, predation by larger raptors like the goshawk (Accipiter gentilis), and collisions with man-made structures. The interplay between the female's larger body size, which confers a competitive advantage in territory defense during the winter months, and the male's smaller size, which reduces daily energy requirements, is a central axis of the species' life-history strategy.
